Entre politiques et vécus – cartographie: Between Policy and Lived Experience: Mapping Real Inclusion in Montréal
À Montréal, une carte collaborative révè: In Montréal, a collaborative map reveals inclusive places based on immigrants’ lived experiences, to help people find their way around the city.
Au Café la Ligne verte, une participante: At Café la Ligne verte, a participant stops in front of the project poster: “Montréal traced by the lived experiences of its diversity.” Photo: Melissa Vaitiligame
Cet article est né d’un décalage qui rev: This article grew out of a gap that comes up often in the field: there is a lot of talk about inclusion in Montréal, but less about how it is actually lived in everyday places. Between public policy and the real experience of people arriving in the city, there is a space that is rarely documented. That is where the organization AFS Interculture Canada put its finger.
Le 19 mars, je suis allé à la rencontre: On March 19, I went to meet the participants in their project “Montréal tracée par les vécus de sa diversité” (Montréal traced by the lived experiences of its diversity) at its launch evening. I listened to their stories, talked with the project leads, and watched how this map took shape from very concrete experiences: looking for a place, feeling like you belong there, understanding the city piece by piece.
J’ai ensuite croisé ces récits avec les: I then cross-referenced these accounts with the information available on the project and its context, in particular the City’s equity, diversity and inclusion policies, to understand what this tool actually changes, or reveals.
L’objectif n’est pas de faire le tour de: The goal is not to cover the whole question of immigration or inclusion in Montréal. It is simpler: to show how, for those who arrive, the city is built from specific places, and why this dimension often remains a blind spot.
Ce que vous vous apprêtez à lire repose: What you are about to read rests on partial but situated experiences, and that is precisely where something is at stake.
<strong>À Montréal, une carte prend form: In Montréal, a map is taking shape from stories. Not an administrative map, nor an urban promotion tool, but a lived-in map, shaped notably by young people from immigrant backgrounds who talk about their relationship to places, between rootedness, obstacles and reappropriation.
<strong>Le 19 mars dernier, l’organisme: On March 19, the organization AFS Interculture Canada presented the project “Montréal tracée par les vécus de sa diversité.” It is a collective tool that offers a reading of Montréal from the perspective of those who move through it, settle in and try to find their place. Behind this initiative lies a specific problem: for many immigrants, the city exists first as a fragmented space that is hard to read, where resources are scattered and landmarks are missing.
Le Café La Ligne Verte, situé rue Ontari: Café La Ligne Verte, on rue Ontario Est between Frontenac and d’Iberville, fills up quickly. Dim lighting, tables close together, low conversations that gradually fade. At the back, a small stage, usually reserved for artists, this time hosts the people behind the project and participants who have come to share their own urban experiences.
Vanessa Valderrama, directrice des compé: Vanessa Valderrama, director of intercultural skills at AFS Interculture Canada, begins by explaining the purpose of the evening. Presented as the culmination of 10 months of work, “<l1>Montréal tracée par les vécus de sa diversité” is an interactive map that lists more than a hundred places deemed inclusive</l1> by their users. There are surely more, and the tool is in fact designed to evolve. It can be added to and corrected so that everyone can make it their own. In any case, behind these geographic points, another issue is emerging: the link between the migration experience and Montréal’s urban space.
Esteban Buongiovanni, directeur général: Esteban Buongiovanni, executive director of AFS; Cyrine Mansri, representative of Place des Arts; and Vanessa Valderrama, project lead. Photo: Melissa Vaitiligame
« L’appartenance ne se décrète pas : ell: “Belonging can’t be decreed: it is built, place after place.” This idea, conceived by the map’s initiators, structures the project. For an immigrant, the city does not exist from the outset as a coherent whole; they first perceive it as a succession of anonymous spaces – an environment where you can live without necessarily belonging.
<strong>Un espace pour dire ce qu’on ne: A space to say what isn’t said elsewhere
Ce type d’initiative s’inscrit dans le c: This kind of initiative is part of the broader equity, diversity and inclusion (EDI) policy adopted by the City of Montréal to promote territorial equity, access to services and the fight against discrimination.
Mais ces objectifs reposent sur une cond: But these objectives rest on a condition that is rarely spelled out: people must still know where to go, which places to turn to and how to find their way around the city. The concrete legibility of the territory is precisely the blind spot the project seeks to fill.
Le projet est réalisé dans le cadre de l: The project is carried out under the <l1>Montréal inclusive 2025-2026 call for projects</l1>, launched by the City of Montréal and the ministère de l’Immigration, de la Francisation et de l’Intégration (MIFI), with an overall budget of $4 million for the entire Montréal territory. The goals of the initiative include fostering harmonious intercultural relations and fighting racism and discrimination. Right in the wheelhouse of AFS Interculture Canada, which has been present in Quebec for nearly 50 years and focuses on developing intercultural skills and youth civic engagement.
L’idée part d’un constat : les jeunes is: The idea starts from an observation: young people from immigrant backgrounds have few spaces to report complex, often ambivalent experiences. “The goal was to create a safe space to talk about difficult topics,” explains Vanessa Valderrama.
<strong>Des ateliers au territoire, la v: From workshops to the territory, the city becomes an experience
Pendant 10 mois, près de 500 participant: Over 10 months, nearly 500 participants aged 18 to 35 took part in more than 40 workshops on the themes of racism, discrimination, intercultural communication and stereotypes, says the project lead.
Dans la salle, les regards convergent, l: In the room, eyes converge, listening settles in, and laughter sometimes ripples through, at the turn of an anecdote or a lightly tossed-off word. Attention never flags. As the testimonies follow one another, the distance between the stage and the audience shrinks.
Macarena Figueroa, arrivée du Chili il y: Macarena Figueroa, who arrived from Chile less than two years ago, says she discovered the workshops while taking francisation classes. “I was looking for a place to practise French. But it became something else.” That something more is in fact a space where the migration experience can be put into words, shared and pooled, she explains, which remains difficult in the usual institutional settings.
Ce côté concret prend la forme d’une car: That concrete side takes the form of an interactive map, built collaboratively by the participants, on which each person marks meaningful places: those where they felt welcomed, recognized, legitimate. Macarena, for example, adds a library, a community centre and a café in Rosemont that offers discounted food boxes. “Many immigrants face economic hardship. It’s important to know about places like that,” she says.
Arrivé du Sénégal à l’âge de huit ans, S: Souleymane Bouchet, who arrived from Senegal at the age of eight, marks spaces linked to dance on the map, namely studios, parks and public squares. “Dancing is a way of getting together. You can go to Place des Arts, there are always people dancing,” he says. He also mentions the Montréal International Jazz Festival, where “all the communities come together.” These places work as points of convergence in a city that is otherwise segmented.
Pour Esteban Bongiovanni, directeur géné: For Esteban Bongiovanni, executive director of AFS Interculture Canada, the stakes go beyond simple mapping. “It’s about giving participants the chance to leave a mark, both individual and collective.” That mark comes through a shift in how the city is seen, so that places are no longer merely functional but become vessels of experience.
<strong>Une ville fragmentée, des points: A fragmented city, identifiable points of contact
Le projet ne pointe pas explicitement la: The project does not explicitly point to the city’s social and cultural fragmentation, which means communities often coexist without fully meeting. But by offering spaces for dialogue and mapping inclusive places, the map implicitly shows that such places are lacking or not visible enough. “We wanted to create connections,” explains Vanessa Valderrama, “between people of different origins, but also with the host society.” The workshops, the cultural outings, the group activities, all of it contributes to that connection.
Un autre témoignage repris par la respon: Another testimony relayed by the project lead describes a clinic where a hard-of-hearing person felt welcomed despite their apprehensions. This kind of story reveals a central point: inclusion depends not only on the measures in place, but on how they are concretely carried out in specific interactions. Each point on the map thus becomes a micro-narrative.
La carte ne résout pas les inégalités st: The map does not resolve structural inequalities or unequal access to resources. It depends on voluntary contributions and cannot claim to be exhaustive. But it brings forward a function missing from public policy: a lived, immediately usable reading of the territory.
Pour les nouveaux arrivants, la carte ré: For newcomers, the map addresses this lack of legibility and works as a shortcut, cutting the time needed to identify reliable places that others have tried and tested.
Pour les organismes et les institutions,: For organizations and institutions, it acts as a mirror, making inclusive practices visible, but also their absence, by introducing a form of informal assessment of inclusive practices based on real experience rather than stated intentions. “The goal is also to prompt reflection: why am I not on this map?” says Vanessa Valderrama. Finally, for participants, it is a form of recognition of their contribution, which becomes a useful and transferable resource.
Un autre enjeu apparaît dans les témoign: Another issue emerges in the testimonies: scattered information. “There are a lot of resources for immigrants, but they’re hard to find,” Macarena points out. The map acts here as a direct remedy to this structural problem.
En fin de rencontre, les chaises se dépl: At the end of the evening, chairs shift, and groups re-form around drinks and small bites. While some log on to the map to set their own personal landmarks, the conversations carry on, continuing from what has just been said.
La carte agit comme une interface entre: The map acts as an interface between individual journeys and urban space. It makes legible a process that is often invisible, the gradual building of a sense of belonging, not through speeches, but through concrete places.
Entre les objectifs institutionnels et l: Between institutional objectives and the reality on the ground, it occupies an in-between space: that of the real uses of the city.

Et le projet ne s’arrête pas à la parole: And the project doesn’t stop at speaking out; it turns speech into a tool. “We didn’t want the conversations to just vanish into thin air. The idea was to move toward something concrete,” M<sup>s</sup>. Valderrama explains in an interview.
Une activité illustre particulièrement b: One activity captures this shift from lived experience to action especially well: blackout poetry. Working from news articles that cast immigration in a negative light, participants were invited, Ms. Valderrama recalls, to black out with a marker the words they rejected and keep only the ones they wanted to work with. From these preserved fragments, new texts emerge: poems built out of discourse that was stigmatizing to begin with. The gesture is simple but formative: turning a discourse imposed on them into material they’ve reclaimed.
